text: An employee's identity now reaches on-prem AD and Entra ID. But plenty of hybrid organizations also run real workloads on AWS — and without a plan, that becomes a third, disconnected identity island instead of part of the same hybrid story.

The problem shows up the moment an organization uses more than one AWS account, which is the norm — separate accounts for production, development, security, and logging, isolated on purpose. Without a centralized approach, an administrator ends up creating a separate IAM user in every single account, each with its own password, and removing someone's access means hunting them down account by account when they leave.

AWS IAM Identity Center — formerly AWS SSO — is AWS's answer: one centralized hub for workforce access across every account in an AWS Organization. Administrators define permission sets, assign them to users or groups for specific accounts, and a person signs in once at the Identity Center access portal to see every account and role they've actually been granted, with no separate IAM credentials per account.

Identity Center doesn't have to manage its own user directory at all — it can federate to an external identity provider over SAML, commonly Entra ID or Okta. When it's federated to the same Entra ID tenant an organization already uses for Microsoft 365 and Azure, that tenant becomes AWS's source of truth too. The same group membership that was synced up from on-prem AD now also determines AWS access, so there's one identity across on-prem, Azure, and AWS instead of three separate ones.

That closes the loop on hybrid identity: one account, created once, reaching every environment it needs to. Chapter 2 turns to a different question entirely — Zero Trust, and why identity itself becomes the perimeter once a network stops being the thing you can trust by default.
